title: An HR assistant employees can trust

text: An HR assistant employees can trust
Evidence-based answers and controlled actions

Which policy applies?
How much leave do I have?
What happens when I submit?

Bootcamp milestone project
Nusantara Digital is fictional. All demo data is synthetic.

0:00–1:00 | The problem

An HR assistant needs to do more than give a convincing answer. It needs to use the correct policy, protect employee information, and handle requests safely.

This bootcamp project is set at Nusantara Digital, a fictional company. All employee records and policies in the demo are synthetic. Imagine an employee who wants to take annual leave. They first need to understand the policy, then check their remaining balance, and finally submit a request. Those steps involve different kinds of information and different levels of authority.

The intended benefit is easier employee self-service. I have not measured time savings or business impact. My goal here is to demonstrate a working workflow and show the evidence behind its behavior.

Source: HR-Agent/brief.md; HR-Agent/rubric.md.
The solution and implementation scope
Policy questions
Answers with retrieved policy sources
Personal balance
Records tied to the authenticated employee
Leave proposals
Explicit confirmation creates a pending request

Provided: UI, datasets and contract models
Implementation: backend, retrieval, tools, safety controls, evaluation and Docker delivery

1:00–2:00 | Solution and contribution

The application supports three parts of the employee journey. Policy questions use retrieved documents and citations. Balance questions read the authenticated employee's records. Leave requests begin as proposals, which the employee reviews and explicitly confirms.

In this project the Streamlit interface, datasets, UI contract, and Pydantic contract models are provided. The implementation work covered the FastAPI backend, hybrid retrieval, the bounded agent and its tools, action validation, telemetry, evaluation, and Docker delivery.

The interface communicates with the API rather than reading the database directly. This matters because the backend can apply the same identity and validation rules to every request.

I will now show one employee journey. Notice when the application is answering a question and when it is preparing an action.

Presenter preparation: describe personal or team ownership accurately. The scope here follows the assignment and repository, not an independently verified authorship audit.

6:00–7:30 | Architecture

The Streamlit interface sends a bearer token and the user's message to FastAPI. FastAPI resolves the employee identity and validates the request. The agent chooses from four permitted tools: policy search, personal balance, preparing a leave proposal, and creating an HR ticket.

For policy questions, retrieval combines keyword matching with meaning-based search in PostgreSQL with pgvector. The results are combined and reranked. The assistant can cite documents retrieved in that run. Indexing preserves document versions and section metadata. Redis caches retrieval results. PostgreSQL remains the source of truth, so losing the cache should affect performance rather than ownership rules.

The lower path is the key action boundary. The user explicitly confirms a proposal through the API. The backend checks ownership, expiry, dates, annual-leave notice, current balance, and overlap in a transaction before writing a new pending request. A successful idempotent replay returns the original request. The model cannot approve leave.

Telemetry records limited metadata for traces and monitoring. Documents and model output are untrusted inputs and cannot establish employee identity.
Source: HR-Agent/src/retrieval.py; HR-Agent/brief.md; HR-Agent/templates/demo-script.md.
Engineering decisions that control behavior
Evidence before answers
Retrieved sources, valid citations and abstention
Identity from the backend
Prompts cannot choose whose records to access
Confirmation before submission
Owner checks, expiry and duplicate prevention
Approval remains a human responsibility.

7:30–9:00 | Engineering decisions

First, use retrieved evidence for policy answers. RAG means the assistant retrieves relevant policy passages before answering. Hybrid retrieval combines keyword matching with meaning-based search, then ranks the results. This helps with both specific policy terms and different ways of asking the same question. A valid citation is necessary, but it does not prove that every sentence follows from the source.

Second, bind personal-data tools to backend authentication. The balance tool does not accept an employee ID from the model. A prompt asking for another employee's data must not grant that access.

Third, separate preparation from commitment. Preparing a proposal validates dates, working days, overlap, leave type, balance, and three-weekday advance notice for annual leave using the Jakarta date. Confirmation checks the proposal again at the action boundary. Idempotency means retrying the same confirmation does not create a second leave request.

The backend also distinguishes policy questions from action requests. Carry-over and diagnosis-channel questions retrieve evidence and cannot write actions; recognized medical disclosures are blocked. Pattern detection remains limited and is not universal medical-text detection.

A bounded agent can choose from a small set of tools within execution limits. These constraints reduce the scope of mistakes, while tests check whether the controls actually hold.
Source: HR-Agent/brief.md; HR-Agent/src/retrieval.py; HR-Agent/tests/test_confirmation_boundary.py.

title: Recorded results and a lesson learned

text: Recorded results and a lesson learned
Lesson: policy entitlement and personal balance need different tools.
October 19 metrics only; citation validity does not prove full support. Oct 22: 6 QA cases pass locally in both languages; database verification pending.

9:00–11:00 | Evaluation, monitoring and learning

This table summarizes the saved evaluation from October 19, 2026. All 15 scenarios passed, including the required hard gates. Citation validity was 100 percent under the implemented checks. Median latency was about 4.03 seconds, and p95 latency was about 4.95 seconds. These figures describe this small run. They are not a claim of universal accuracy or production readiness.

The report also records full retrieval recall under a document-trace proxy. That proxy is not an independent ranking evaluation. Citation validity does not establish semantic entailment, and estimated monetary cost was not configured.

One useful failure involved the difference between annual leave entitlement and remaining balance. An early live test selected the balance tool for an entitlement question. The agent instructions were refined to separate policy allowance from personal balance, and the same live test passed afterward. This is why I test the tool choice as well as the final wording.

Optional recent lesson, replacing part of the earlier example: A broad request classifier mistakenly treated a carry-over question as leave preparation. We narrowed it and tested policy questions alongside action requests. Live checks also caught a missing tool-call/result pairing that scripted tests had missed; we fixed it and added an assertion.

Open slide 15 briefly, or show the live monitoring screen. Explain latency, error rate, and tool calls. Traces use limited metadata and redaction. An abstention may contribute an error category, so an alert requires interpretation. Return to slide 7.

Source: HR-Agent/templates/evaluation-report.md; HR-Agent/submission-evidence/step11/evaluation_report.json; HR-Agent/submission-evidence/step11/ui-monitoring.png.

QA01 and QA04–09 remain unverified in this update. Deployed PostgreSQL verification remains pending. These results are separate from the October 19 pass-rate claim.

11:00–12:00 | Closing

This is an educational system using synthetic data and demo bearer tokens. A real deployment would need production identity management and stronger operational controls. The evaluation covers 15 scenarios. Broader adversarial tests, independent answer-quality checks, and load tests would provide stronger evidence.

Human manager review remains outside the application. The agent only creates pending requests. The repository records local Docker verification and cloud deployment preparation, while the Render and Neon verification document still lists hosted deployment and cloud checks as pending. I am not claiming a verified public deployment.

The regex intent classifier is only for demo purposes. It gives predictable handling for selected patterns, but it can miss paraphrases and misunderstand negation or messages with multiple intents. For example, "Jangan approve cuti saya, saya hanya ingin tahu prosedurnya" still matches the approval pattern and triggers a refusal. Requests classified as normal continue to the LLM, so a missed regex match does not necessarily mean the final answer is wrong.

The next step is to replace the regex intent classifier with LLM-based classification using structured output for intent and required fields. We will evaluate paraphrases, negation, and multiple-intent messages, including Indonesian and English examples. Authentication, business-rule validation, and explicit confirmation will remain enforced by the backend. Other next steps are production authentication, broader evaluation, and a verified deployment with backup and recovery checks.

My main learning was that building an AI application requires more than connecting a model. Retrieval, access control, validation, and evaluation are what make its behavior dependable.

Thank you. I am happy to discuss the implementation or the tests.
